extracted.intended_audience: historians, moral philosophers, and students of moral historiography
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative principles for writing or interpreting moral history and for judging the moral character of individuals, classes, and nations across historical stages of civilisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not infer immorality from illegitimate birth statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Judging a nation's immorality by the number of illegitimate births is fallacious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statistics exclude prostitution and miss important contexts: retrospective marriages that 'legitimise' past relations, customary permanent unions without ceremony, and legislative impediments to marriage (e.g., Sweden). Quantitative counts cannot distinguish causes or forms of sexual behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate types of sensuality
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise qualitative differences in sensuality across peoples (coarse/cynical, dreamy/aesthetic, furtive/retiring) rather than treating all as a single vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different forms of the same vice produce widely different effects on public disposition and cannot be captured by blunt metrics; moral analysis should describe the character and social effects of each form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for climatic and environmental influences on morals
rubrics_metrics.description: Climate indirectly shapes morals by affecting life patterns (indoor vs outdoor), the distribution of beauty, and social habits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Northern beauty linked to delicacy of complexion and class stratification; southern beauty is more democratically diffused. Such differences influence manners and sexual morals and must be considered in comparative moral judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise civilisation's mixed effects on sexual virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Refined civilisation tends to foster sensuality, while rude/semi-civilised societies often display stricter observance of sexual virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Urban wealth and public amusements increase temptation; industrial pursuits can encourage self-restraint but also postpone marriage, increasing temptation. Historical examples: Irish early marriage promoting chastity but harming economic prudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral change is not uniformly improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Societies may gain some virtues and lose others as civilisation advances; moral 'improvement' is rarely unmixed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain virtues die away with progress (e.g., heroic self-sacrifice), and each stage retains distinctive excellence. Analysts should weigh gains against losses rather than assuming linear moral progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge virtues produced by adverse conditions (war, oppression)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conditions like war or national oppression elicit magnanimous virtues (heroism, self-sacrifice, fraternity) that may diminish in peaceful, industrial ages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although war is evil, it historically cultivates certain noble moral qualities; moral history should note virtues' contextual origins rather than dismissing their source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value diversity of civilisation types
rubrics_metrics.description: Different states, classes, and institutional forms (small states, monastic orders, heterogeneous empires, class representation) preserve distinct moral excellences valuable to humanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political or social uniformity can erode moral variety; historians should recognise the corrective social functions of monasticism, small states, and class-based representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not equate intellectual with moral progress
rubrics_metrics.description: High intellectual or material civilisation does not guarantee greater moral excellence; some intellectual conditions may undermine certain virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great cities and enlightenment foster crime repression, social and intellectual virtues, and industrial virtues, but often weaken self-sacrifice, reverence, and chastity. Analysts must avoid assuming moral superiority where intellectual achievement is high.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give weight to practical pursuits over mere opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Intellectual causes often influence morals indirectly by shaping habits and pursuits; the moral life is more governed by ways of living than abstract opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A type of virtue is first produced by circumstances and only later rationalised into doctrine; historians should trace how occupations, social organisation, and habits create moral dispositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish private from political moral standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals may display higher private probity while excusing or committing political dishonesty or violence; political approvals are a poor guide to general moral sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid rigid inferences from political rhetoric or actions to a people's private morals; political crimes may be intertwined with national virtues such as submissiveness that enable despotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid attributing corporate faults to all members
rubrics_metrics.description: Characteristics visible in a corporation or institution (e.g., ecclesiastical persecutions) should not be taken as conclusive of the private virtues of its individual members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional actions are often the most conspicuous historical records; moral historians must seek the less visible charitable, educational, and pastoral labours of clergymen that history overlooks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use nation-relative standards for assessing virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: National virtues derive from differing motives and histories; applying one nation's moral measure to another leads to serious misconception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: French national virtue based on sympathy and expansive intellectual sympathy; Anglo-Saxon virtue based on duty and moral rectitude. Comparative moral judgment must consider each nation's moral foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise grouping and trade-offs among virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtues cluster (heroical, amiable, industrial, intellectual), and prominence of one group often diminishes prominence of others; balance of elements defines a moral type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One cannot impose a single model of perfection across types; moral evaluation should assess whether a character is 'perfect of its own kind' rather than measuring all by one ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the rudimentary virtue of an age
rubrics_metrics.description: Each period and society has a rudimentary virtue—an essential quality that grounds moral excellence and by which moral indifference may be judged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rudimentary virtues vary (e.g., patriotism in ancient republics, chastity for women in England, truthfulness in industrial societies). Moral historians should discover and use the period's rudimentary virtue as a key evaluative axis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist moral intolerance and ethnocentrism
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid reducing all characters to the model of one's own tastes or virtues; failure of imagination and vanity lead to unjust denigration of different moral types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historians should be aware that people more readily sympathise with imperfect characters of their own type than with superior characters of other types; cultivate imaginative understanding across types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider interaction of innate temperament and circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: An individual's moral type results from both native temperament and external social conditions; mismatches limit development of natural virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how social institutions, education, and dominant models encourage or suppress certain temperaments; moral histories should account for lost potentials produced by unfavourable environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate religions as moral teachers in context of their age
rubrics_metrics.description: Religious moral teachings are effective only when they align with prevailing social tendencies; misaligned teachings will be abandoned, refined, or neglected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historians should analyse which parts of religious moral systems persist or change according to their conformity with contemporary social forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote empirical study of bodily causes of moral dispositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocate studying physical and medical causes of moral predispositions (moral pathology) to better understand and possibly treat moral disease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of relevant phenomena: effects of disease, castration, insanity, nervous illnesses, and physical development on character. Such study would complement historical analysis and clarify questions about race, climate, and temperament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trace external causes and modifications of moral types
rubrics_metrics.description: A moral historian should trace how external circumstances produce, modify, impair, or destroy moral types over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The historian's task is to examine the external influences on morals, the ideal types proposed in different ages, their realisation in practice, and their transformations—rather than assuming static morals.
